title: Design and Optimization of MEMS Variable-Area Capacitive Pressure Sensors for Improved Sensitivity and Linearity in Fingertip Tactile Sensing
abstract: This paper presents the design, modeling, and optimization of MEMS-based capacitive pressure sensors utilizing three variable-area mechanisms: a movable dielectric, an asymmetrical movable plate, and a symmetrical movable plate. By utilizing changes in capacitor area instead of changing the distance between plates, these configurations, these configurations minimize the trade-off between sensitivity and linearity found in conventional diaphragm-based sensors. Analytical modeling based on solid mechanics and electrostatics, alongside finite element simulations in COMSOL Multiphysics, was used to characterize diaphragm deflection and capacitance response. Parametric analysis revealed that a symmetric movable plate with a diaphragm thickness of 0.04 mm and a pillar width of 0.1 mm yielded optimal performance, achieving sensitivities of 2.3811 fF/kPa (analytical) and 2.72805 fF/kPa (simulation), with nonlinearities of 0.0697% and below 2%, respectively. A 10×10 sensor array with specifications based on Harmon’s design criterion demonstrated consistent performance across varying pressures, validating the design’s suitability for robotic, prosthetic, and biomedical applications requiring high sensitivity, linearity, and array compatibility.

title: Modeling Electrode and Microchannel Geometry for Detection of Cadmium (Cd), Lead (Pb), and Copper (Cu) in Drinking Water through a Capillary-Driven Microfluidic Electrochemical Sensor
CIDR Mirror Lab Framework: Strengthening Graduate-Level IC Design Education
Performance Analysis of Encoding Schemes in Hyperdimensional Computing for EEG Signals
abstract: Hyperdimensional computing (HDC) is a ‘brain-like’ system that represents data using high-dimensional vectors, or hypervectors. It performs simple bitwise operations on these hypervectors, enabling efficient classification in tasks such as biosignal applications. A major challenge in HDC is the encoding of analog signals into hypervectors. In seizure detection, features from the electroencephalogram (EEG) signal are typically extracted prior to encoding. Common features include local binary patterns (LBP), spectral power, line length, and mean amplitude. While these features have been individually evaluated in terms of classification accuracy, their comparative hardware performances remains largely unexamined. This work presents a comparative analysis of various encoding schemes for seizure detection, evaluating their classification accuracy, area, and energy efficiency. Among the approaches considered, single, distinctive features such as LBP are determined to be the most efficient choice for seizure detection, achieving 86.1% sensitivity and 71.7% specificity. In contrast, continuous-valued features like spectral power and line length offer less accuracy, while combining multiple features with LBP increases specificity by 6.7% but at the cost of 195% increase in area and a 309% increase in energy.

title: A Dual-Mode AZO-Based Surface Acoustic Wave Temperature Sensor in Single-Phase Unidirectional Transducer Configuration
abstract: This study reports the development and characterization of a dual-mode surface acoustic wave (SAW) temperature sensor fabricated on a Si(100) substrate with a thermally grown SiO2layer and an RF -sputtered aluminum-doped zinc oxide (AZO) piezoelectric film. A single-phase unidirectional transducer (SPUDT) with a wavelength of$72 \mu \mathrm{m}$was employed to enhance signal directivity and reduce insertion loss. The design targeted a Rayleigh-mode fundamental frequency in the 50-100 MHz range. The fabricated sensor was wirebonded onto a gold-traced PCB and characterized using a vector network analyzer, revealing a fundamental mode at 76.76 MHz and a higher-order mode at 5.48 GHz at room temperature. Thermal response testing was conducted using a hot air source, with surface temperature monitored by a thermal imaging camera. Frequency downshifts were observed with increasing temperature for both modes. The fundamental Rayleigh mode exhibited a sensitivity of 77.5 kHz /° C, a temperature coefficient of frequency (TCF) of −1009 ppm /° C, and a non-linearity of 3.46%. The higher-order mode showed a sensitivity of 800 kHz /° C, a TCF of −145 ppm /° C, and a non-linearity of 4.88%. These results highlight the potential of AZO-based SAW sensors for passive temperature sensing in thermally dynamic environments and across various wireless communication bands.

title: Design Space Exploration of Precision-Scalable Convolutional Neural Network Accelerators for Edge Device Inference
abstract: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) deployed on edge devices must meet strict constraints on power, area, and performance, but their compute and data movement demands make this difficult. We present a precision-scalable CNN accelerator architecture with a novel MISO-FIFO for edge inference, supporting 8-, 4-, 2-bit operations. We explore 200 design configurations by varying three architectural parameters: memory bus width, systolic array size, and FIFO depth. After pruning designs exceeding 3.75 mm2, 39 configurations are synthesized using 22 nm FD-SOI technology. Our analysis shows workload-dependent trends: depthwise layers work best with smaller arrays, shallow FIFOs, and wider memory buses, while pointwise layers perform better with larger arrays and deeper FIFOs. The best designs achieve 13.65 GOPS at 26.74 GOPS/W and 5.83 GOPS/mm2and for depthwise optimal, and 108.94 GOPS at 129.45 GOPS/W and 35.57 GOPS/mm2for pointwise optimal, running at 0.8 V and 300 MHz. Reducing precision from 8 to 2 bits provides a 1.41 times average compute speed-up, at the cost of reduced accuracy. These findings guide workload-aware accelerator design selection tailored for edge-device constraints.

title: Delay Mismatch Optimization in Routing Dominated Multi-Path Systems: A Case Study on an IR-UWB Edge-Combiner Transmitter Front End
abstract: Routing-dominated multi-path architectures play a critical role in enhancing data throughput and resource efficiency in computing, communication, and RF systems. Hence, ensuring matched point-to-point signal arrival is critical to minimizing distortion, latency, and data corruption while managing increased routing density and interconnect complexity. In this paper, delay mismatch in routing-dominated systems is investigated while assuming negligible mismatch within circuit blocks. A variancebased framework is proposed to quantify and optimize the delay mismatch components across multiple levels of abstraction: the system, block, and layout. To validate this model, systematic routing optimization techniques are applied to an impulse-radio ultra-wideband (IR-UWB) edge-combiner transmitter front end (TFE) operating at $6.5-8.0 \mathrm{GHz}$ center frequency. The TFE requires precise pulse widths in the picosecond range, making it highly susceptible to interconnect-induced delay variability. After optimization, the total variance of propagation delay was decreased by 94.37% based on post-layout simulations.

title: A Temperature-Stabilized Gm Technique for Folded-Cascode OTAs in 22nm FDSOI Technology
Optimizing TinyEngine for the RISC-V Vector Extension
abstract: Embedded edge devices face strict energy and size constraints for IoT and WSN applications. Because of this, advances have been made to enable state-of-the-art edge neural network models, such as MobileNetv2, to decrease their peak memory requirements to tens to hundreds of kilobytes using network architecture search tools and highly optimized libraries. However, optimization work in this space has been limited to a specific set of microcontroller cores including the recently developed embedded RISC-V processors that can take advantage of the highly parallel nature of machine learning workloads. This work explores the optimization of the TinyEngine inference library for the T908 vector processor as a reference for embedded vector processor designs. The vectorization achieved a 2.83x speedup relative to a scalar portable version of TinyEngine running on the same core, without a corresponding fall in average accuracy. In addition, replacing floating-point quantization with fixed-point operations is shown to have only a minor 3-4% reduction in Top 5 accuracy with negligible impact on performance, indicating that integer-only vector implementations can also be viable for embedded machine learning workloads.

title: A Reconfigurable Variable-Precision Bipolar/Binary QR-based IMC Accelerator in 22nm FDSOI
abstract: In-memory computing (IMC) hardware is crucial for enabling low-power neural network (NN) inference on edge devices. The charge redistribution (QR) IMC compute model dominates state-of-the-art (SOTA) IMC hardware implementations. However, existing QR IMC implementations are inflexible in terms of supportable bit-precisions and weight data types. On the other hand, different NN models have been found to require different optimal bit-precisions for energy efficiency. Additionally, challenges such as VTHvariations arise in deeper tech nodes. Here, we introduce a variable-precision QR-based IMC accelerator based on a 10T1C bitcell that supports both bipolar and binary weights. We achieve a maximum energy efficiency close to recent SOTA at 516 TOPS/W, 409.6 GOPS at a compute SNR of 21.03 dB.

title: An Energy-Aware Q-Learning for Cluster-based Routing in WSNs
abstract: As sensor nodes are typically battery-powered or rely on energy harvested from the environment, recent works on the development and deployment of large-scale wireless sensor networks (WSNs) focus on reducing power consumption to improve network lifetime. Determining optimal routing for data to take the least energy path, or avoid non-responsive and energy-depleted nodes improves the lifespan of WSNs. Thus, we explore routing algorithms with computational intelligence that consider routing distance and residual energies of neighboring sensor nodes, while remaining energy-efficient. In this work, we present an energy-aware cluster-based routing protocol that leverages reinforcement learning. Our simulations show that using a simple Q-learning algorithm improves the energy efficiency of the network by more than 2x as compared to a traditional clustering algorithm. By incorporating energy awareness into the routing decisions, the operational lifetime of the network is improved by 1.4x. However, this leads to prioritizing routes with higher energy levels, which may not always be the shortest, resulting in a trade-off in energy efficiency. This work demonstrates the potential of reinforcement learning for developing energy-efficient routing protocols in wireless sensor networks.

title: Low Power SAR ADC with Adaptive Resolution for ECG Applications
abstract: This paper presents a 10-bit successive approximation register analog-to-digital converter (SAR ADC) that utilizes adaptive resolution for electrocardiogram (ECG) applications. For lower power consumption, we take advantage of the sparsity of the ECG signal to reduce the number of operations performed by the ADC. The SAR ADC utilizes most significant bits tracking that adaptively switches between full switching mode (FSM) during periods of high activity and reduced switching mode (RSM) during periods of low activity. In FSM, the ADC operates as a regular SAR ADC, while in RSM, the SAR ADC performs fewer approximation comparisons, thereby reducing power consumption. This adaptive resolution scheme achieves a Walden Figure-of-Merit (FoM) of 112.042 fJ/conv-step, which is 54.260% lower when compared to an unmodified SAR ADC Walden FoM of 244.952 fJ/conv-step.

title: An All-Back-Gate Input Nauta-OTA for a 3rd-Order GM-C Ladder-Type Filter in 22nm FDSOI with Improved Linearity
abstract: This paper presents an all-back-gate input Nauta-OTA for a$G_{m}-C$filter in a fully depleted silicon-on-insulator (FDSOI) CMOS technology. Due to the rising challenge in designing analog circuits, especially for filters in a newer technology and in a lower voltage domain, a technique using back-gate control is utilized to improve the linearity. A feature that makes an all-back-gate input viable is the ultra-thin body and box (UTBB) in FDSOI that enhances electrostatic properties of the CMOS technology and creates additional transistor devices. In this paper, the proposed all-back-gate input technique for Nauta-OTA improves the linearity of the$G_{m}-C$filter, achieving a THD of -50.4dB and an IIP3 of 19.52dBm while consuming$\mathbf{51.04}\mu \mathbf{W}$, suitable for low-power circuit applications.

title: A Fully On-Chip Differential Charge Amplifier in 22nm FDSOI for MEMS-Based Piezoelectric Pressure Sensors
abstract: This paper presents a fully on-chip differential charge amplifier for microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) piezoelectric sensors in 22nm fully-depleted silicon-on-insulator (FDSOI) technology. MEMS piezoelectric sensors generate small charge signals in response to mechanical stress which requires a highly sensitive and low-noise charge amplifier to accurately convert the signal. A charge amplifier topology is adopted, using an N-boosted folded-cascode operational transconductance amplifier (OTA) and a fully differential difference amplifier (FDDA) with back-gate common-mode feedback (CMFB) circuits as main stages. The proposed design also incorporates pseudo-resistors and on-chip capacitors in the feedback network to maintain the desired impedance while ensuring compact integration. Post-layout simulations confirm the high performance of the system blocks, achieving a 93.3-dB open-loop gain and 94.1-MHz gain-bandwidth for the gain stage, and a small-signal attenuation of 296.6 mdB with a 458-MHz bandwidth for the driver stage. The integrated charge amplifier achieves a closed-loop gain of 45.6 V/V, a high-pass cutoff frequency of 70.8 Hz, and consumes$\mathbf{285.6}\ \mu \mathbf{W}$. These results validate the design's suitability for high-precision, low-power MEMS sensor interfaces.

title: Peripheral Block Extension of a Reconfigurable 8T SRAM In-Memory Computing Macro for High-Throughput MAC Operations
abstract: In-Memory Computing (IMC) is a solution to data-transfer bottlenecks by allowing computations within the memory itself. 8T SRAM bitcells are used in a digital IMC architecture for improved read stability and immunity to noise and process variations. Among the state-of-the-art digital 8T SRAM IMC works is the Bit-Parallel Searching and Computing In-Memory (BP-SCIM) macro that supports the most number of operations - content-addressable memory (CAM) search, Boolean logic, and arithmetic. Its bit-parallel approach allows for linear-time multiplication and division, and separate compute and write cycles give a higher clock frequency than other works. However, it only supports multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations by separate multiplication and addition operations, reducing its efficiency. Hence, in this work, the macro was reimplemented under the GlobalFoundries (GF) 22 nm FDSOI CMOS technology, achieving a lower latency, higher throughput, and a maximum operating frequency of 900 MHz in arithmetic operations. The macro was also extended with a peripheral block that improved the performance in MAC operations, decreasing the latency and increasing the throughput by 156 % with an average energy efficiency of 4.86 GOPS/W.

title: Comparative Analysis and Implementation of Energy-Quality Scalable Multiply-Accumulate Architectures for TinyML Applications
abstract: Recent trends in machine learning algorithms have shifted from computer vision applications to near-sensor intelligent data analytics, such as wireless sensor nodes, which are considered as ultra-low power devices. This shift presents new challenges in energy consumption, throughput, and area budgets. This work implements and optimizes Bit Fusion, a 2D-scalable divide-and-conquer (D&C) MAC architecture with precisionscaling from 8 to 2 bits, through bitwidth optimizations and by trading-off complexity overheads that are not aligned with the target MobileNet-v2 model. The designs are synthesized using 22-nm FD-SOI CMOS technology. It was determined that the throughput trade-offs of 1-level architectures in$\mathbf{2 b} \times 2 \ \text{b}$mode for$\mathbf{1 7. 3 7 \%}$less energy per operation and$\mathbf{2 6. 8 4 \%}$more throughput per area would be preferred. Architecture variations were also explored wherein sum-together (ST) architectures outperformed sum-apart (SA) architectures with$\mathbf{2 1. 0 3 \%}$reduction in energy per operation and$\mathbf{3 3. 3 2 \%}$increase in throughput per area.

title: Utilization of TST-MRAM in a Hyperdimensional Associative Memory
abstract: This paper presents the integration of toggle spin torque random access memory (TST-MRAM) in the associative memory (AM) for a more energy-efficient hyperdimensional computing (HDC) architecture. The proposed AM is composed of a TST-MRAM array connected to loser-takes-all comparators, which function together as memory and classifier. The model exploits the differences in capacitor discharge times for the different classes in determining the most similar class. We implement the TST-MRAM-based AM in GlobalFoundries 22 nm FD-SOI technology, with language classification as the target application. Our results show that the proposed model performs a single query faster than the conventional CMOS-based AM. However, it is less energy-efficient due to the inherently low ON/OFF resistance ratio of TST-MRAM cells, resulting in a 7.75x reduction in energy-delay product. Despite this, we project that the proposed model is able to outperform the conventional CMOS-based AM when memory cells with higher inherent resistances are developed.

title: A Low-Power Fully-Differential Chopper-Stabilized LNIA in 22nm FD-SOI for MEMS-based Thermopile Sensors
abstract: This paper presents an analog front-end interface circuit composed of a fully-differential, chopper-stabilized, lownoise instrumentation amplifier (LNIA) for MEMS-based thermopile sensors in 22 nm FD-SOI technology operating at a 0.8 V supply. A fully-differential architecture was chosen to provide a broader full-scale range for the succeeding processing stages with the given supply voltage. This configuration utilizes the inherent thermopile output resistance as the LNIA input resistor, allowing for precise gain control of the amplifier gain to accommodate thermopile devices with varying output voltages. In this specific study, the LNIA was designed to operate as a readout circuit for a differential thermopile sensor modeled in COMSOL Multiphysics. The modeled thermopile sensor generates an output voltage in the range of $\mathbf{6 1 2} \mu \mathrm{V}$ to 4.9 mV and has an equivalent resistance of $51.6 \mathrm{k} \Omega$. The proposed chopper LNIA demonstrates an input-referred noise density of $53.9 \mathrm{nV} / \sqrt{H z}$, representing a $\mathbf{9 9. 9 7 \%}$ reduction in noise of the base amplifier without chopping. This noise performance was achieved while maintaining a low power consumption of $31.2 \mu \mathrm{~W}$ when operating at a chopping frequency of 67 kHz, with an NEF of 12.98. This study shows promising implementation of a chopper-stabilized LNIA for low-energy applications, making it suitable for MEMS-based thermopile sensor systems.

title: Design of a Low-Power LNIA-ADC Interface Circuit in 22nm FDSOI for a Thermopile Sensor in Biomedical Application
abstract: This paper presents a design of a low-noise instrumentation amplifier (LNIA) and analog-to-digital converter (ADC) interface in 22 nm FDSOI for infrared (IR) sensingin biomedical applications. The LNIA is used as a signal conditioning block for a thermopile sensor input and utilizes a capacitively-coupled chopper instrumentation amplifier (CCIA) topology with a ripple reduction loop (RRL). The ADC adopts a successive approximation register (SAR) topology to digitize the signal from the LNIA with a power-gated counter D flip-flop array and a split binary weighted (SBW) capacitive digital-toanalog converter (CDAC). Schematic simulation shows that the interface circuitconsumes $1.65 \mu \mathrm{~W}$ of power and can output a digital signal that represents a data set from a temperature range of $25^{\circ} \mathbf{C}$ to $45^{\circ} \mathbf{C}$ with a step of 200 mK.

title: A Hyperdimensional Computing Architecture with 4.4x Energy Efficiency in 65nm CMOS
abstract: Hyperdimensional computing (HDC), a brain-inspired computing defined on high-dimensional vectors (or hypervectors), has emerged as a promising energy-efficient approach for solving classifications tasks. Current HDC architectures typically rely on binary dense hypervectors with approximately equal number of 1 and 0 elements. While these provide good classification performance, they may suffer from high energy consumption due to high switching activity, especially with hypervectors whose dimensionality is in the thousands. In this work, we explore the use of binary sparse representations, in which most of the elements are 0s, for a highly energy-efficient HDC architecture. We consider a language classification task as a case study, targeting 65nm CMOS process. Our results show a remarkable 4.4x reduction in energy and 3.68% reduction in area at iso-performance as compared to when using dense representations. Furthermore, increasing the sparsity in the architecture leads to increased classification accuracy and energy efficiency.

title: MPPT-Controlled Adaptive Reconfigurable 5.8GHz RF Energy Harvesting Front-End in 65nm CMOS
abstract: The range of input power levels that allow a RF energy harvester to produce an output level required to power a WSN node is limited. The limitation is caused by the losses arising from the static configuration of the RF energy harvester that is not ideal for a wide range of input power levels expected from RF energy sources. A dynamic RF energy harvester where both the matching network and rectifier are reconfigurable to adapt to the input power level improves the sensitivity and provides voltage regulation, extending the operating range. To implement this, the number of stages in the rectifier cascade and the input impedance produced by the matching network are modified. Several configurations could produce the required output, but the most efficient configuration for different input power levels is chosen using a Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT) mechanism to maximize the power harvested from RF sources. Simulation results for a design implemented in 65nm CMOS process show an improvement of around 17dB in dynamic range and up to 20% in efficiency for a dynamic RF energy harvester implementing MPPT compared to a static RF energy harvester in producing a 1V output using a 5.8GHz input. Silicon test results show that the performance of the dynamic rectifier is close to simulated results at around -8dBm, 5.8GHz RF input while providing a form of voltage regulation at high power input that increases dynamic range and removing the need for large voltage limiter circuits.

title: Comparative Modeling of Four-Ended, Modified Four-Ended, and Double-Ended Beam MEMS Thermopile Sensor Structures for Functional Area Optimization
abstract: Research on infrared thermopiles has seen substantial advancements in fabrication techniques and material synthesis in order to maximize the thermoelectric performance of the sensors. In the field of microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) where space optimization is key to effective miniaturization, determining the optimal layout for thermopile elements within specific area constraints is of high importance. This study presents a comparative modeling of three beam-type thermopile structures to maximize the output voltage for a given functional area. Four-ended beam (FEB), modified FEB, and double-ended beam (DEB) thermopile structures and the subsequent variations in their component dimensions were modeled analytically and through finite element simulation to determine the optimal variation for each structure. DEB was the standout structure with an optimal configuration possessing an absorber size of $2.304 \times 10^{5} \mu m^{2}$ and displaying an output voltage of $6.158~{mV}$, responsivity of $295.537 \mathrm{~V}/\mathrm{W}$, detectivity of $1.321 \times 10^{8} {~cm} * {~Hz}^{1 / 2} * {~W}^{-1}$, and a time constant of $61.58{~ms}$ from an input power of $80 {~W}/{m}^{2}$. The optimal configurations of the FEB and modified FEB achieved output voltages of $3.783~{mV}$ and $3.679~{mV}$, respectively.

title: Federated Learning with MLPerfTiny Tasks and Server-side Momentum
abstract: Federated learning can bring significant benefits to edge IoT systems in their scalability, efficiency, and application space by increasing the amount of computing for the nodes while decreasing the amount of network traffic required. On the other hand, the rise of efficient techniques in TinyML has been a significant boon for ultra low-power IoT ML sensors. Sadly, works on federated learning either use standard networks that are too large for TinyML devices, or are applied to relatively easier tasks to compensate for the performance degradation. In this work, we model federated learning on all four of the MLPerfTiny tasks with their respective baseline models and show that applying federated learning to TinyML models causes significant performance degradation. We also show that the performance degradation is exacerbated when the number of nodes increases. Finally, to address the performance degradation without compromising the original task or increasing the computational load for the client devices, we propose adding momentum to the server-side learning optimizer and show that this significantly mitigates the performance degradation effect, again reaching MLPerfTiny standards on all tasks.

title: A 9-bit 2MS/s Set-and-Down Monotonic SAR ADC in 22nm-FDSOI for MEMS-based Thermoelectric Sensor Readout Interface Circuit
abstract: This paper discusses the design and performance of a set-and-down monotonic SAR ADC in 22nm-FDSOI. The designed 9-bit, 2MS/s SAR ADC has a simulated ENOB of 8.94 bits, SNDR of 55.57dB, SFDR of 70.10dB, and a total power consumption of 7.86μW. The achieved FoM for the SAR ADC is 8.02fJ/conv-step. The SAR ADC design is suitable as data converters for MEMS-based thermoelectric sensor readout interface circuits.

title: FPGA-targeted optimization approaches for SVM and CNN human activity recognition models using the HARTH and HAR70+ datasets
abstract: Human activity recognition (HAR) has been explored extensively for decades as a use case of machine learning (ML) in low-power embedded applications such as FPGAs. While most existing research has focused on development of classical ML models, recent work targets deep ML models for their capacity to learn effectively on low-quality, noisy datasets. As these models have been widely developed for improved accuracy and recently produced publicly available free-living datasets such as HARTH and HAR70+ have started targeting the issue of reliable annotations, our challenge of interest is model deployment. This study explores optimization approaches specifically for resource-limited FPGA deployment applications. We evaluate their trade-offs in model performance and resource utilization estimates after high-level synthesis (HLS) of representative classical (SVM) and deep (CNN) learning models. Axis and data format reduction were most effective in balancing model performance and resource utilization with single-axis models consuming half the resources estimated for our unoptimized models.

title: Passive 5.8GHz RF Energy Harvester in 65nm CMOS
abstract: This paper presents a passive 5.8GHz RF Energy Harvester (RFEH) implemented in 65nm CMOS technology that allows batteryless operation and reduction in overall size of WSN and IoT sensor nodes, which are limiting more widespread implementation. The RFEH consists of an on-chip matching network and optimized rectifier that are co-designed for maximum efficiency and sensitivity in the RFEH in gathering the required energy for the load circuit. The passive 5.8GHz RFEH prototype demonstrated a sensitivity of around -13dBm in gathering enough energy to produce 0.5V on a 10uF capacitive load, allowing the harvested energy to be reasonably combined with energy from other sources. When used as the only energy source, the ability to gather and provide a continuous supply of 8uW (10uA at 0.8V) is demonstrated, which is enough to power low-power RF circuits such as OOK and FSK receivers without the need of any battery, allowing batteryless operation.

title: 10 Gb/s Energy-efficient Optical Transceiver using 1060 nm HCG MEMS-tunable VCSEL in 28 nm FD-SOI Technology
abstract: The 28 nm FD-SOI CMOS technology was proven to be faster and more power efficient due to greater control of the threshold voltage of transistors. An optical transceiver was designed in this node for a 1060 nm HCG MEMS-tunable VCSEL to transmit information at a higher data rate and reduced energy consumption. The transmitter block is composed of a binary-to-thermometer encoder and CA cascode driver slices. The PAM-4 modulation scheme was used to directly modulate the VCSEL, and a multimode fiber (OM5) that can transmit the required data rate was modeled. For the receiver block, a RCG TIA was used followed by a decoder to recover the input bit streams. The optical transceiver designed and implemented achieved the required data rate of 10 Gb/s, an approximate BER of $10^{-15}$, energy efficiency of 0.785 pJ/bit, and an eye diagram containing three clear eyes, each with a peak-to-peak voltage of greater than 70 mV.

title: An EEG Analog Front-End Unit for Wearable Applications Implemented in 28nm FD-SOI
abstract: An instrumentation amplifier (IA) and low-pass filter (LPF) for an electroencephalogram (EEG) analog front-end (AFE) unit were designed for wearable devices using non-contact electrodes (NCE) with very high impedance in the gigaohm range. The IA consists of a low-noise amplifier, a high-pass filter, chopping circuits, and a capacitive impedance boosting loop that increases the IA’s input impedance to match the NCE. An LPF that minimizes the IA’s output chopping ripple was realized as an active Gm-C 3rd-order Butterworth filter using low-GmOTA’s. The EEG AFE achieved a 0.5 Hz to 109 Hz bandwidth in simulations with a passband gain of 37.05 dB. It also achieved an input impedance of 2.53 GΩ @ 100Hz and an input referred noise of 2 μVrms. Lastly, the system’s total power consumption is 6.5 μW using a 1 V supply.

title: A 288 nV/∕∥ Hz Low-noise Capacitively-coupled Instrumentation Amplifier (CCIA) in 22-nm UTBB FD-SOI for Signal Conditioning of MEMS Piezoresistive Pressure Sensors
A high CMRR, high input impedance current-feedback instrumentation amplifier (CFIA) in 22-nm UTBB FD-SOI for signal conditioning of MEMS piezoresistive pressure sensors
abstract: A current-feedback instrumentation amplifier (CFIA) with chopper stabilization (CHS) was designed using a standard 22-nm UTBB FD-SOI process. The CFIA serves as part of the signal conditioning block for a piezoresistive pressure sensor and is composed of three subblocks, which were implemented using a fully-differential difference folded cascode, a single-ended folded cascode, and a class-AB common-drain push-pull amplifier. The IA has a 141dB open-loop gain, a 243dB CMRR, and a $29\mathrm{G} \Omega$ input impedance. It operates at 0.8 V supply voltage and consumes $15 \mu \mathrm{W}$ of power. The input-referred noise is $5 \mu \mathrm{V} /$ Hz without CHS and $1 \mu \mathrm{V} /$ Hz with CHS.

title: Comparison of Hardware-optimized CNN and SVM Models for Human Activity Recognition using the HARTH and HAR70+ Datasets
Energy-Efficient Sparse Hyperdimensional Computing for Speech Recognition
abstract: This study proposes an energy-efficient hyperdimensional computing (HDC) architecture for speech recognition. Energy efficiency is achieved through the use of 1) sparse hypervectors, 2) architecture co-optimized for optimal accuracy-energy trade-off, and 3) redundancy pruning. Sparse hypervectors contribute to computational efficiency by reducing the number of 1s in the hypervectors. Implementing and optimizing segmentation in the architecture enables processing only a portion of the hypervector at a time, promoting hardware reuse, thus reducing both area and energy usage. The integration of redundancy pruning significantly conserves energy by disabling bit positions in hypervectors that do not contribute useful information during inference. The effectiveness of these techniques is demonstrated using the ISOLET dataset. The base HDC model, employing 4096-bit hypervectors with a hypervector density of 2% and a segmentation size of 128, achieves a classification accuracy of 83.71%. With redundancy pruning, the proposed model maintains the same accuracy while eliminating 45.43% redundant bit positions, resulting in 2.26% energy savings per query and 1.02x enhanced energy efficiency at the cost of 11.68% increase in area.

title: Integration of In-Memory Computing Capabilities to a Self-Matching Complementary-Reference Sensing Scheme for TST-MRAM
abstract: The study proposes an in-memory computing (IMC) implementation to a 2T1MTJ TST-MRAM array while using a fast self-matching complementary-reference (SMCR) sensing scheme. The IMC integration and implementation presented is able to perform bitwise AND/NAND, OR/NOR, XOR/XNOR, and Full Adder (FA) operations. Testing and verification was done on a 2x1 TST-MRAM array using 28nm FDSOI CMOS technology. Overall, the 2x1 array test results show that it can achieve short latency and good energy consumption even with less transistors per bitcell compared to current TST-MRAM IMC implementations. After integrating the IMC module, latencies for bitwise AND/NAND and OR/NOR were recorded to be 2.2x to 3.7x faster compared to 3T1MTJ integrations, with energy consumptions of only 128.75fJ for AND/NAND and 145.15fJ for OR/NOR operations.

title: Performance Analysis of Multistage Cross-Coupled Differential-Drive Rectifiers using Simulations on 65nm CMOS Process
abstract: In this paper, the effect of varying transistor widths, rectifier stages, and threshold voltage on the performance of cross-coupled differential-drive rectifiers using a 65nm CMOS process are observed through simulations with a resistive load. Improving conversion efficiency has mostly been the focus for radio frequency (RF) rectifiers used in RF energy harvesting (RFEH) where the input power is expected to be small. Input impedance is also another concern since the matching network between the antenna and rectifier may introduce power loss due to reflections. However, it has been difficult to accurately model and predict the performance and characteristics of these rectifiers because of their non-linearity. Instead of relying on calculations, data from simulations is used to summarize the effects of various design decisions and come up with a suitable design given target specifications. Results show that the same output specifications can be achieved with less rectifier stages by using higher threshold transistors. This design achieves approximately the same conversion efficiency at the same input power level with a higher input resistance which helps increase the voltage gain for impedance matching networks for the rectifier.

title: Redundancy Pruning for Binary Hyperdimensional Computing Architectures
abstract: Hyperdimensional computing (HDC) is an emerging memory-centric computing paradigm that uses vectors with very high dimensions as distributed representations in associative memories. HDC architectures are energy-efficient compared to conventional artificial neural networks because it uses simple operations. However, HDC architectures still contain massive bitwise operations and a large memory footprint. Current optimizations often reduce dimensions to consume lower energy at the cost of degraded accuracy. In this work, we propose pruning redundant bits in the associative memory because these bits do not contribute any information during classification. Reducing these irrelevant bit-wise operations results in significant energy savings without sacrificing accuracy. We tested the pruning of redundant bits on three applications: character recognition, hand-written digits recognition, and DNA sequencing classification problems. We achieved a speedup of 1.2x-3.4x and 14%-66% energy savings per prediction at the cost of a 6.4%-17.9% increase in area.

title: Properties and Design of CMOS Thyristor Delay Elements
abstract: The CMOS thyristor delay element and its basic operation are presented in this paper. Six variations of the thyristor design developed over the years to extend the delay length, to improve the consistency of the delay, or to control the sensitivities of the delay are also discussed. This includes the complementary thyristor, the thyristor without the current source, the thyristor with threshold elevation, the thyristor with opposing current source, the single-ended thyristor, and the thyristor-type feedback delay element. Design considerations common to all CMOS thyristors are also discussed to provide insights on topology selection, capacitive loading, and transistor sizing.

title: Indirect stress and air-cavity displacement measurement of MEMS tunable VCSELs via micro-Raman and micro-photoluminescence spectroscopy
abstract: Abstract We employ micro-Raman spectroscopy to optically infer the stress experienced by the legs of a bridge-type microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) used in high contrast gratings tunable vertical cavity surface emitting lasers (VCSELs). We then employ micro-photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy to indirectly measure the air cavity displacement of the same MEMS structure. Results from micro-Raman showed that electrostatically actuating the MEMS with a DC bias configuration yields increasing residual stress on the endpoints of the MEMS with values reaching up to 0.8 GPa. We simulated a finite element model via Comsol Multiphysics which agrees with the trend we observed based on our micro-Raman data. Our micro-PL spectroscopy showed that change in the air cavity of the VCSEL structure resulted in a change in the full width of the PL peak emitted by the layer consisting of four pairs of distributed Bragg reflectors. The change in the full width of the PL peak was due to the change in the optical cavity induced by displacing the MEMS via externally applied bias and agrees with our transfer matrix convolution simulation. These optical characterization tools can be used for failure analysis, MEMS design improvements, and monitoring of MEMS tunable VCSEL devices for mass production and manufacturing.
